title: Harold's dance-band jobs from Bucktown to the La Vida
summary: Long account of the Peking Inn, Tom's Roadhouse, Buzzy Williams and Charlie Fishbein bands, Tom Anderson's, his marriage and leaving in 1924, playing again from 1929.

bands.name: Buzzy Williams and Charlie Fishbein's band

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: Dick Denner went to work out at a place called the Peking Inn out in Bucktown. It was Chinese food, you know. Well out in Bucktown, you know, the big thing that people went out there for was to play the slot machines, you know, and dance and of course, Sproonings was more or less a fine rest, a family type of restaurant, Sproonings was, and of course people used to come out there to dance, you know what I mean, and play the slot machines and that's what they had all out there in Bucktown was slot machines, a lot of people went out there for that. So I went to work for well, it's Chinese food, the Peking Inn, and after I worked for them all quite a while, then one night they came to me and they had two bosses, the piano player was a half owner, and he said to me, you know man, he said we can get a piano player and a drummer and the drummer sings for them, just what would we pay you? I said, well man, you know I don't sing, I said, so you're going to have to get you that piano player and drummer. So then I took a band myself over the Tom's Roadhouse, I couldn't get a union musician to go out there either, it was on the West End Shell Road, so I had to get some non-union musicians to work with me out there, but there used to be other musicians to come in and sit in, you know, sit in, and Raymond used to, Raymond talks about it every night, he said, you remember when I used to come out there when you had a job out there, Tom's Roadhouse? I said, yeah, that's a long time ago, 1920 then, and then I went to work with, with Buzzy Williams and Charlie Fishbein, I worked at the Arcadia Ballroom, that was ballroom dancing, and that incidentally became the first, after about a year after we left, it became the first Nicola dance hall in town. Then I went to work with, or I went to work with the Buzzy and Charlie at the Cadillac, I stayed all the time with them, there were changes made in between, I stayed with them at the Cadillac, then I went to Bucktown, Joe Julien's with them, then I went to Tom Anderson's on Rampart between Canal and Iverville, they had two Tom Anderson's, you know, one was on the corner of Basin and Iverville, then the other Tom Anderson, you know, the Tom Anderson place, but on Rampart between Canal and Iverville, then I went to the La Vida. Oh, I got married when we were working at the Tom Anderson, and the funny thing, well of course in them days they used to feed you the musicians, you know, of course like, we'd always have, like two would go at a time, you know, I'd always had music on the stand there, and the cook at Tom Anderson, she said to me, she said, how are you getting married? I said, yeah. I said, well it's not going to be a big wedding, I told her. She said, well where's it going to be? I said, St. Joseph Church. She said, well I'll tell you, she said, there might not be anybody else there, she said, but I'll be there, the cook said. Sure enough, she was there. Then I worked at La Vida, I went to the La Vida with them, and of course we were in the music business, and I was married too, and my wife was scared to stay up at the store at night, don't blame her, stay upstairs, you know. So I used to have to take her home to her mother's every night and sleep. So I played, stayed there up, well into 1924, and then a friend of mine, I left my drums over there for him, I said, I'm going to leave the job, I just gave my two weeks notice and I said, if you want, I said, you can take the job, I said, I know you'll be able to stay on the job with him, I said, use my drums as long as you want. So he went over there and he showed that he was quite good by it for quite a while. And I didn't play too much then, I played just, hmm, just once in a while or something like that, you know, spots, maybe a parade or something. And I didn't start playing again until 1929, then when I went to work at Stale at the place called the College on Ramport between Canal and, out between Conti and Biennual there. And then of course, I, oh yeah, in the 30s, I believe I went down and played with the Peep of Cope, his band down in the Green Mill, just for a week, I didn't want to really, I didn't want to play too much anymore after
